plan.paradox: A razor sells itself. And you never buy the blade.
plan.odd_fact: In 1903 Gillette sold 51 razors but 168 blades  -  far more blades than handles.
plan.twist: But it does a job  -  it turns every razor into a blade subscription.
plan.cause: The starter kit forces the first purchase, then the razor-only option creates a lifelong blade demand; 90,884 razors sold in 1904 came with 123,648 blades, proving the model.
plan.everyday: Barber shop: Basic shave $5, no razor; Premium shave $20, razor + a few blades; Unlimited plan $25, razor once, blades refilled monthly  -  the unlimited plan feels smart because you already own the razor.
plan.rule: If the first buy is a tool, expect recurring costs. Follow for more.

beats.say: A razor sells itself. And you never buy the blade.
A starter kit, a razor plus a few blades.
A premium set, razor, many blades, and a case.
A subscription, razor once, blades delivered forever.
In 1903 Gillette sold 51 razors but 168 blades. Looks wasteful.
But it does a job - it forces you to keep buying.
Each razor sold creates a lifelong blade customer.
In 1904 the company sold 90,884 razors and 123,648 blades, a blade per razor and then some.
You see it everywhere. A barber offers a basic shave for $5, no razor.
A premium shave for $20 includes a razor and a few blades.
An unlimited plan for $25 gives the razor once and refills blades forever - it feels cheap because the razor is already yours.
If the first buy is a tool, expect recurring costs. Follow for more.
